Floating-point addition is not associative because modern hardware represents real numbers with finite precision. In exact arithmetic, changing the grouping of additions does not change the result: adding a to b and then adding c is equivalent to adding a to the sum of b and c. In floating-point arithmetic, however, each intermediate result usually must be rounded to the nearest representable value. Since the two groupings create different intermediate values, they can incur different rounding errors and produce different final answers.

The effect is especially visible when numbers have very different magnitudes. If a very small number is added to a very large number, the small contribution may fall below the precision available at the large number’s scale and be rounded away. If several small numbers are added together first, their combined value may become large enough to affect the later addition. Cancellation also matters: subtracting nearly equal values can remove leading significant digits, making prior rounding errors comparatively important.

Large matrix multiplications repeatedly compute dot products, each of which is a reduction of many products into a sum. Although the mathematical result is independent of the order in which those products are accumulated, the floating-point result is not. A simple sequential implementation may add terms from left to right. A vectorized CPU implementation may form several partial sums in SIMD lanes and combine them afterward. A multithreaded library may assign blocks to different threads, while a GPU may use a tree-shaped parallel reduction. Tiling, thread scheduling, hardware generation, compiler optimization, and library version can all change the effective reduction order.

Fused multiply-add instructions introduce another source of variation. They compute a product and an addition with a single final rounding, whereas separate multiplication and addition normally round twice. Fused operations are often more accurate, but they need not match results produced without fusion.

Consequently, two implementations of the same matrix multiplication can produce entries that differ by a few units in the last place, and errors may be larger for long or ill-conditioned dot products. Such differences can propagate through later calculations, particularly iterative algorithms or computations near decision thresholds. This does not usually indicate a hardware fault; it is an expected consequence of finite-precision arithmetic.

Bitwise reproducibility therefore requires controlling more than the input data. It may require a fixed reduction tree, deterministic thread scheduling, consistent use of fused operations, identical precision and rounding modes, and reproducible numerical libraries. These constraints can reduce performance because they limit parallelism and implementation freedom. When exact reproducibility is unnecessary, applications commonly compare results using justified numerical tolerances rather than requiring identical bits.
